title: For the Hopelessly Impatient
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article addresses people whose impatience persists despite years of conventional advice, deep breathing, meditation, perspective-taking, because urgency and excitement still overwhelm their self-regulation. Rather than fighting the urge to rush, the author proposes redirecting it: instead of slowing down while waiting, impatient people should speed up at something else entirely, throwing full intensity into an unrelated task or activity until the original trigger passes. The piece frames this as using a person's own weakness, the drive for immediate action, as the mechanism for coping with delay, rather than suppressing it. It closes with the line that sometimes turning a weakness against itself is what makes a person stronger.
points: Conventional advice like deep breathing and perspective-taking often fails chronically impatient people because urgency overwhelms their self-regulation.
The proposed fix isn't to slow down but to redirect intensity toward an unrelated task, fully occupying attention until the impatience trigger passes.
The strategy works by feeding the desire for immediate, intense action rather than fighting or suppressing it.
The piece frames this as turning a personal weakness (impulsive urgency) into the very tool that manages it.
quotes: Impatient people simply can’t wait. They want to hear the news, achieve the outcome, and talk through the problem right NOW.
Self-regulation evaporates under the heat of urgent, excitable, or stressful situations.
Instead of slowing down and waiting for what they want to know, do, or achieve, cravenly impatient people need to speed up at something else.
The idea is not to fight your desire for impatience but to feed it.
Sometimes, using a weakness against itself makes us stronger.
